title: Ombré striped triangle shawl
subtitle: A top-down DK triangle with garter stripes shading from dark to light across the wingspan.
excerpt: A top-down triangular shawl in DK wool, worked in plain garter stitch with garter stripes graduating from a deep colour at the neck to a pale colour at the cast-off edge. No stranded colourwork: carry one colour and break it, then pick up the next. Wingspan 145 cm, centre-back depth 68 cm. About 80 g each of five graduating DK shades.
sourceNotes: Garter stripe shawls are a simple construction with no single definitive source. Top-down triangular shawl with garter stripes follows Elizabeth Zimmermann, Knitting Without Tears (1971), §Shawls, with a multi-shade graduating palette added as a contemporary application.

knitting.gaugeText: 22 sts × 44 rows = 10 × 10 cm in garter stitch on 4 mm needles, blocked.
knitting.finishedSizeText: Wingspan 145 cm. Centre-back depth 68 cm. Blocked.

glossaryTerms.definition: A small strip of garter stitch worked on a few stitches, rotated and picked up to form the centre-back starting point of a top-down triangle shawl.

Leaving the unused yarn attached at the edge when working two or more alternating colours, so it can be picked up again on the next section without cutting. Works when the colours are used again within a few rows.

content.text: A top-down triangular DK shawl with five graduating garter stripe shades, from darkest at the neck point to palest at the cast-off edge. Wingspan 145 cm, depth 68 cm. The shawl begins with a
garter tab
and grows on the standard top-down schedule. No stranded colourwork: each shade is used for one section of approximately 30 RS rows before breaking and picking up the next shade.
Each shade section grows by 4 stitches per RS row, so the sections visibly widen as the colours lighten. For a
colour carry

effect between adjacent shades, leave the previous shade attached at the edge and carry it up for 4 rows before breaking. Budget about 80 g (about 175 m / 190 yards) each of five graduating DK shades.
What you need

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 4 mm (UK 8 / US 6) circular needle, 80 cm or longer

content.text: Gauge

22 stitches and 44 rows to 10 cm over garter stitch on 4 mm needles, blocked. If all five shades are from the same yarn line, gauge should be consistent. If shades are from different yarn lines, swatch each shade; a 2-stitch-per-10-cm gauge difference between shades creates a visible width step at the colour transition.
Stitches used
Pattern
Garter tab
Work the garter tab in shade 1: 3 sts on waste yarn, 6 garter rows, pick up 9 sts. Place markers: after st 1, after st 5 (centre), before st 9.
Shade sections (each approximately 30 RS rows)
RS row: k1, yo, SM, yo, k to 1 st before centre marker, SM, yo, k1, yo, SM, k to last st, yo, k1. (4 sts added per RS row)
WS row: k all sts.

Work shades in order: 30 RS rows of shade 1, 30 RS rows of shade 2, 30 RS rows of shade 3, 30 RS rows of shade 4, 20 RS rows of shade 5. Break and join each shade at the start of its section. Do not carry over shades that are more than 4 rows apart.
Bind off
Work Jeny's surprisingly stretchy bind-off in shade 5.
Stitch count check-ins
End of shade 1 (30 RS rows): 9 + 120 = 129 stitches. Wingspan approximately 30 cm.
End of shade 4 (120 RS rows total): 9 + 480 = 489 stitches. Wingspan approximately 111 cm.
Common faults

Colour join visible as a bump: two strands were knotted together at the transition rather than being woven in separately. Work the last row of one shade with a 15 cm tail; work the first row of the next shade with a 15 cm tail; weave each tail in separately along the selvedge on the WS.

Colour sections unequal width in the finished shawl: the sections with more rows are visibly wider because the shawl grows 4 stitches per RS row. For a perfectly even graduated band, each shade section should be the same number of RS rows.
Blocking
Wet-block to wingspan 145 cm and depth 68 cm. All five shades should be confirmed colourfast before soaking together.
Care
Hand wash in cool water, lay flat to dry.
What to try next

Try a reverse ombré: palest at the neck, darkest at the cast-off edge. The wider sections at the outer edge carry more of the dark shade, making the colour band visually larger at the bottom than at the top.
